title: 13. Scaling to Millions: Scaling to Millions of Users — The Complete Playbook
summary: This is the most important section. Don't optimize early — optimize at the right time.
objectives: Everything You Need to Actually Handle 1M, 10M, 100M+ Users

sections.title: 1. The Scale Playbook
sections.body:
### What to Change at Each Growth Stage

This is the most important section. Don't optimize early — optimize at the right time.

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ USERS     │ WHAT BREAKS                │ WHAT TO DO                 │
├───────────┼────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┤
│ 0 - 1K    │ Nothing                    │ Single server, monolith    │
│           │                            │ Focus on building features │
│           │                            │ PostgreSQL is enough       │
├───────────┼────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┤
│ 1K - 10K  │ Slow DB queries            │ Add indexes                │
│           │ Repeated computations      │ Add Redis caching          │
│           │                            │ Connection pooling         │
│           │                            │ Move slow tasks to Celery  │
├───────────┼────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┤
│ 10K - 50K │ Single server CPU maxed    │ Add Nginx + load balancer  │
│           │ DB connections maxed       │ 2-3 app servers            │
│           │                            │ PgBouncer (conn pooler)    │
│           │                            │ Rate limiting              │
├───────────┼────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┤
│ 50K - 200K│ DB reads are bottleneck    │ Read replicas (2-3)        │
│           │ Single point of failure    │ Redis Cluster              │
│           │ Deployment = downtime      │ Blue-green deployments     │
│           │                            │ CDN for static assets      │
│           │                            │ Monitoring (Prometheus)    │
├───────────┼────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┤
│ 200K - 1M │ Monolith is too big        │ Split into 3-5 services    │
│           │ DB writes are bottleneck   │ Message queues (Kafka)     │
│           │ Need independent scaling   │ CQRS (read/write split)    │
│           │                            │ Auto-scaling               │
│           │                            │ Distributed tracing        │
├───────────┼────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┤
│ 1M - 10M  │ Single DB can't hold all   │ Database sharding          │
│           │ Global latency             │ Multi-region deployment    │
│           │ Feature changes are risky  │ Feature flags              │
│           │                            │ Canary deployments         │
│           │                            │ Chaos engineering          │
├───────────┼────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┤
│ 10M+      │ Everything at limits       │ Full microservices         │
│           │                            │ Custom CDN / edge compute  │
│           │                            │ Dedicated teams per service│
│           │                            │ Event-driven everything    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### The #1 Mistake

```
❌ WRONG: "We'll have millions of users, let's build microservices + Kubernetes NOW"
   → 6 months of infrastructure, zero users, startup dies

✅ RIGHT: Build monolith → Get users → Scale when something breaks
   → Instagram scaled a Python/Django monolith to 100M users before refactoring
   → Twitter ran on Ruby monolith until 2012 (300M users)
   → Start simple. Scale what breaks.
```

sections.title: 2. Real Benchmarks
sections.body:
### How Many Requests Can Your Stack Actually Handle?

```
Single Server (4 CPU, 8GB RAM):

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Framework / Config          │ Requests/sec │ Concurrent     │
├─────────────────────────────┼──────────────┼────────────────┤
│ Flask + Gunicorn (4 workers)│ 1,000 - 3,000│ ~200           │
│ FastAPI + Uvicorn (1 worker)│ 3,000 - 8,000│ ~5,000         │
│ FastAPI + Gunicorn (4 work) │ 8,000 - 20K  │ ~20,000        │
│ FastAPI + 4 servers + Nginx │ 30K - 80K    │ ~80,000        │
├─────────────────────────────┼──────────────┼────────────────┤
│ Redis GET                   │ 100K+        │ Single thread  │
│ PostgreSQL simple SELECT    │ 10K - 50K    │ With pooling   │
│ PostgreSQL complex JOIN     │ 500 - 2,000  │ Depends on data│
│ MongoDB simple find         │ 20K - 80K    │ With sharding  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Key insight:
  1M daily active users ≠ 1M simultaneous requests

  Typical pattern:
    1M DAU → ~100K peak hourly → ~1,700 peak per minute → ~28 requests/sec

  That means: Even a single FastAPI server handles 1M DAU for simple APIs!

  BUT: If each request hits DB, does AI inference, or streams data,
       the math changes dramatically. That's when you need scaling.
```

### When You Actually Need More Servers

```python
# Calculate your scaling needs

daily_active_users = 1_000_000
peak_multiplier = 5              # Peak is 5x average
avg_requests_per_user = 20       # Pages, API calls per session
session_duration_hours = 0.5     # 30 min average session
peak_hours = 4                   # Hours of peak traffic

# Average requests per second
total_daily_requests = daily_active_users * avg_requests_per_user
avg_rps = total_daily_requests / (24 * 3600)  # ~231 req/sec

# Peak requests per second
peak_rps = avg_rps * peak_multiplier  # ~1,157 req/sec

# How many servers needed?
server_capacity = 5000  # FastAPI + Gunicorn per server
servers_needed = peak_rps / server_capacity  # 0.23 → 1 server!

# BUT with database queries (50ms each):
effective_capacity = 1000 / 0.05 * 20  # 20 pool connections = 400 req/sec
servers_needed_realistic = peak_rps / effective_capacity  # ~3 servers

print(f"""
Scaling Calculator:
  Daily Active Users: {daily_active_users:,}
  Avg RPS: {avg_rps:.0f}
  Peak RPS: {peak_rps:.0f}
  Servers needed (CPU-bound): {max(1, int(peak_rps / server_capacity) + 1)}
  Servers needed (DB-bound):  {max(1, int(peak_rps / effective_capacity) + 1)}
""")
```

sections.title: 3. Load Testing
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Simulates a real user browsing your app
- Login when user starts (runs once per user)
- Browse product catalog
- Search for products
- Locustfile.py — Load test your FastAPI app
- Run load test (web UI)
- Run headless (CI/CD friendly)
- Ramp up: Start with 50 users, add 50/sec, up to 1000

### Before launching, you MUST prove your system handles the expected load.

### Tool 1: Locust (Python — Best for Python Developers)

```python
# locustfile.py — Load test your FastAPI app

from locust import HttpUser, task, between

class WebsiteUser(HttpUser):
    """Simulates a real user browsing your app"""
    wait_time = between(1, 5)  # Wait 1-5 seconds between requests

    def on_start(self):
        """Login when user starts (runs once per user)"""
        response = self.client.post("/auth/login", json={
            "email": "loadtest@test.com",
            "password": "testpassword"
        })
        self.token = response.json()["access_token"]
        self.headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {self.token}"}

    @task(5)  # Weight 5 — most common action
    def browse_products(self):
        """Browse product catalog"""
        self.client.get("/products?page=1&limit=20", headers=self.headers)

    @task(3)  # Weight 3 — somewhat common
    def search_products(self):
        """Search for products"""
        self.client.get("/products/search?q=laptop", headers=self.headers)

    @task(2)  # Weight 2 — less common
    def view_product(self):
        """View single product"""
        self.client.get("/products/42", headers=self.headers)

    @task(1)  # Weight 1 — rare
    def add_to_cart(self):
        """Add item to cart"""
        self.client.post("/cart/items", json={
            "product_id": 42, "quantity": 1
        }, headers=self.headers)

    @task(1)
    def view_profile(self):
        self.client.get("/users/me", headers=self.headers)
```

```bash
# Install
pip install locust

# Run load test (web UI)
locust -f locustfile.py --host=http://localhost:8000

# Run headless (CI/CD friendly)
locust -f locustfile.py \
    --host=http://localhost:8000 \
    --users 1000 \
    --spawn-rate 50 \
    --run-time 5m \
    --headless \
    --csv=results

# Ramp up: Start with 50 users, add 50/sec, up to 1000
# Watch: RPS, response times, failure rate
```

### Reading Load Test Results

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Key Metrics to Watch:                                        │
│                                                              │
│ 1. Response Time (p50, p95, p99)                             │
│    p50 < 200ms  → Good                                      │
│    p95 < 500ms  → Acceptable                                │
│    p99 < 1000ms → Edge case OK                              │
│    p99 > 2000ms → RED FLAG 🚨                               │
│                                                              │
│ 2. Requests Per Second (RPS)                                 │
│    Stable under load → Good                                 │
│    Drops as users increase → Bottleneck found!              │
│                                                              │
│ 3. Error Rate                                                │
│    < 0.1% → Production ready                                │
│    0.1-1% → Needs investigation                             │
│    > 1%   → Not ready for production                        │
│                                                              │
│ 4. Where It Breaks (the inflection point)                    │
│    500 users → fine                                         │
│    1000 users → response time doubles → THIS is your limit  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Tool 2: k6 (For More Realistic Scenarios)

```javascript
// load-test.js — k6 script with stages

import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

export const options = {
  stages: [
    { duration: "2m", target: 100 }, // Ramp up to 100 users
    { duration: "5m", target: 100 }, // Stay at 100 for 5 min
    { duration: "2m", target: 500 }, // Ramp up to 500
    { duration: "5m", target: 500 }, // Stay at 500 for 5 min
    { duration: "2m", target: 1000 }, // Ramp up to 1000
    { duration: "5m", target: 1000 }, // Stay at 1000 for 5 min
    { duration: "2m", target: 0 }, // Ramp down
  ],
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<500"], // 95% of requests < 500ms
    http_req_failed: ["rate<0.01"], // Error rate < 1%
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get("http://localhost:8000/products?page=1");
  check(res, {
    "status is 200": (r) => r.status === 200,
    "response time < 500ms": (r) => r.timings.duration < 500,
  });
  sleep(1);
}
```

```bash
# Install k6
# Windows: choco install k6
# Mac: brew install k6

# Run
k6 run load-test.js
```

sections.title: 4. Rate Limiting Algorithms
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Allow 100 requests per minute per IP.
- Tracks exact timestamp of each request.
- Imagine a bucket that holds tokens. - Tokens are added at a fixed rate (e.g., 10/second) - Each request consumes 1 token - If bucket is empty →…
- Rate limit based on user's subscription tier
- Remove old entries outside the window
- Count requests in current window
- Set expiry on the key
- Get current bucket state

**Defines:** `fixed_window_limiter()`, `sliding_window_limiter()`, `TokenBucket`, `rate_limit_middleware()`, `tiered_rate_limiter()`

### How ChatGPT, Stripe, and Twitter Prevent Abuse

### Algorithm 1: Fixed Window Counter (Simple)

```python
import redis.asyncio as redis
from fastapi import Request, HTTPException
from datetime import datetime

r = redis.from_url("redis://localhost:6379")

async def fixed_window_limiter(request: Request, limit: int = 100, window_sec: int = 60):
    """
    Allow 100 requests per minute per IP.

    Problem: Burst at window boundary
      Minute 1 (last second): 100 requests ✅
      Minute 2 (first second): 100 requests ✅
      = 200 requests in 2 seconds!
    """
    client_ip = request.client.host
    window = datetime.utcnow().strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M")
    key = f"ratelimit:{client_ip}:{window}"

    count = await r.incr(key)
    if count == 1:
        await r.expire(key, window_sec)

    if count > limit:
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=429,
            detail="Rate limit exceeded. Try again later.",
            headers={"Retry-After": str(window_sec)}
        )
```

### Algorithm 2: Sliding Window Log (More Accurate)

```python
import time

async def sliding_window_limiter(request: Request, limit: int = 100, window_sec: int = 60):
    """
    Tracks exact timestamp of each request.
    No burst-at-boundary problem.
    Used by: Stripe, GitHub API
    """
    client_ip = request.client.host
    key = f"ratelimit:sliding:{client_ip}"
    now = time.time()
    window_start = now - window_sec

    pipe = r.pipeline()
    # Remove old entries outside the window
    pipe.zremrangebyscore(key, 0, window_start)
    # Count requests in current window
    pipe.zcard(key)
    # Add current request
    pipe.zadd(key, {str(now): now})
    # Set expiry on the key
    pipe.expire(key, window_sec)

    results = await pipe.execute()
    request_count = results[1]

    if request_count >= limit:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=429, detail="Rate limit exceeded")
```

### Algorithm 3: Token Bucket (Most Flexible — Used by AWS, Stripe)

```python
class TokenBucket:
    """
    Imagine a bucket that holds tokens.
    - Tokens are added at a fixed rate (e.g., 10/second)
    - Each request consumes 1 token
    - If bucket is empty → reject request
    - Bucket has max capacity (burst limit)

    Used by: AWS API Gateway, Stripe, most CDNs

    Why it's best:
    - Allows short bursts (burst_size)
    - Smooth rate over time (refill_rate)
    - Simple and memory-efficient
    """

    def __init__(self, redis_client, capacity: int = 100, refill_rate: float = 10):
        self.redis = redis_client
        self.capacity = capacity        # Max burst size
        self.refill_rate = refill_rate  # Tokens per second

    async def consume(self, key: str, tokens: int = 1) -> bool:
        now = time.time()
        pipe = self.redis.pipeline()

        # Get current bucket state
        bucket_key = f"bucket:{key}"
        state = await self.redis.hgetall(bucket_key)

        if state:
            last_refill = float(state["last_refill"])
            current_tokens = float(state["tokens"])

            # Calculate tokens to add since last refill
            elapsed = now - last_refill
            new_tokens = elapsed * self.refill_rate
            current_tokens = min(self.capacity, current_tokens + new_tokens)
        else:
            current_tokens = self.capacity

        if current_tokens >= tokens:
            current_tokens -= tokens
            await self.redis.hset(bucket_key, mapping={
                "tokens": current_tokens,
                "last_refill": now
            })
            await self.redis.expire(bucket_key, 300)
            return True  # Request allowed

        return False  # Rate limited

# Usage in FastAPI
token_bucket = TokenBucket(redis_client, capacity=100, refill_rate=10)

@app.middleware("http")
async def rate_limit_middleware(request: Request, call_next):
    client_ip = request.client.host
    allowed = await token_bucket.consume(client_ip)

    if not allowed:
        return JSONResponse(
            status_code=429,
            content={"detail": "Too many requests"},
            headers={"Retry-After": "10"}
        )

    return await call_next(request)
```

### Per-Tier Rate Limiting (Like ChatGPT/Claude)

```python
TIER_LIMITS = {
    "free":       {"requests_per_min": 10,   "requests_per_day": 100},
    "pro":        {"requests_per_min": 60,   "requests_per_day": 5000},
    "enterprise": {"requests_per_min": 300,  "requests_per_day": 100000},
}

async def tiered_rate_limiter(request: Request, user: User):
    """Rate limit based on user's subscription tier"""
    tier = user.subscription_tier
    limits = TIER_LIMITS[tier]

    # Check per-minute limit
    minute_key = f"rate:{user.id}:min:{datetime.utcnow().strftime('%H:%M')}"
    minute_count = await r.incr(minute_key)
    await r.expire(minute_key, 60)

    if minute_count > limits["requests_per_min"]:
        raise HTTPException(429, f"Rate limit: {limits['requests_per_min']}/min for {tier} plan")

    # Check per-day limit
    day_key = f"rate:{user.id}:day:{datetime.utcnow().strftime('%Y-%m-%d')}"
    day_count = await r.incr(day_key)
    await r.expire(day_key, 86400)

    if day_count > limits["requests_per_day"]:
        raise HTTPException(429, f"Daily limit reached. Upgrade plan for more.")
```

sections.title: 5. Auto-Scaling
sections.body:
### Don't Pay for 10 Servers When You Need 2 at 3 AM

### Docker Compose Auto-Scale (Simple)

```bash
# Scale API to 5 instances behind Nginx load balancer
docker-compose up -d --scale api=5

# Scale down during off-peak
docker-compose up -d --scale api=2
```

### Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (Production)

```yaml
# kubernetes/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: fastapi-app
spec:
  replicas: 3 # Start with 3 pods
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: fastapi-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: fastapi-app
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: myapp:latest
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "250m" # Request 0.25 CPU
              memory: "256Mi"
            limits:
              cpu: "1000m" # Max 1 CPU
              memory: "512Mi"
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8000
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8000
            initialDelaySeconds: 10
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8000
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 10

---
# kubernetes/hpa.yaml — Auto-scale based on CPU usage
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: fastapi-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: fastapi-app
  minReplicas: 2 # Never go below 2 (high availability)
  maxReplicas: 20 # Max 20 pods during peak
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70 # Scale up when avg CPU > 70%
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: memory
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 80 # Scale up when avg memory > 80%
  behavior:
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 60 # Wait 1 min before scaling up
      policies:
        - type: Pods
          value: 4
          periodSeconds: 60 # Add max 4 pods per minute
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300 # Wait 5 min before scaling down
      policies:
        - type: Pods
          value: 1
          periodSeconds: 60 # Remove max 1 pod per minute
```

### Auto-Scaling Visualization

```
              CPU Usage %
  100 ┤
   90 ┤          ╭────╮    ← Scale up at 70%
   80 ┤         ╱      ╲
   70 ┤ ── ── ──╱── ── ──╲── ── ── (threshold)
   60 ┤       ╱           ╲
   50 ┤      ╱             ╲
   40 ┤    ╱               ╲
   30 ┤───╱                 ╲───── ← Scale down kicks in
   20 ┤
      └──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──┬──
     6AM 8  10 12  2  4  6  8 10PM

  Pods:  2   3  5  8  5  3  2  2   ← Scales with traffic
  Cost:  $   $$ $$$ $$$$ $$$ $$ $  ← Pay only for what you use
```

sections.title: 6. Zero-Downtime Deployments
sections.body:
### Your Users Should NEVER See Downtime During Deploys

### Strategy 1: Rolling Update (Default in Kubernetes)

```
State: V1 V1 V1 V1    ← All running version 1

Step 1: V1 V1 V1 [V2]  ← Start 1 new pod with V2
Step 2: V1 V1 [V2] V2  ← V2 healthy → remove 1 V1
Step 3: V1 [V2] V2 V2  ← Continue replacing
Step 4: [V2] V2 V2 V2  ← All running version 2 ✅

Duration: ~5 minutes. Zero downtime.
```

### Strategy 2: Blue-Green Deployment

```
Blue (Current Production):
  ┌───────────┐
  │ Server 1  │ ← Serving live traffic
  │ Server 2  │
  │ Server 3  │ V1.0
  └─────┬─────┘
        │
  Load Balancer ← Points to Blue

Green (New Version):
  ┌───────────┐
  │ Server 4  │ ← New version, running but NOT receiving traffic
  │ Server 5  │
  │ Server 6  │ V2.0
  └───────────┘

Deploy:
  1. Deploy V2.0 to Green servers
  2. Run smoke tests against Green
  3. Switch load balancer: Blue → Green (instant!)
  4. If problems → switch back to Blue (instant rollback!)
```

```python
# blue_green_deploy.py — Simplified blue-green with Nginx

import subprocess

def deploy_blue_green(new_version: str):
    # 1. Deploy new version to green environment
    subprocess.run([
        "docker-compose", "-f", "docker-compose.green.yml",
        "up", "-d", "--build"
    ])

    # 2. Wait for health check
    import time, requests
    for _ in range(30):
        try:
            r = requests.get("http://green-server:8000/health")
            if r.status_code == 200:
                break
        except Exception:
            pass
        time.sleep(2)
    else:
        raise Exception("Green deployment failed health check!")

    # 3. Switch Nginx to point to green
    switch_nginx_upstream("green-server:8000")

    # 4. Keep blue running for 10 min (easy rollback)
    time.sleep(600)

    # 5. Stop old blue servers
    subprocess.run(["docker-compose", "-f", "docker-compose.blue.yml", "down"])

def switch_nginx_upstream(new_upstream: str):
    """Update Nginx config and reload without dropping connections"""
    config = f"""
    upstream app {{
        server {new_upstream};
    }}
    """
    with open("/etc/nginx/conf.d/upstream.conf", "w") as f:
        f.write(config)

    # Graceful reload — existing connections finish, new ones go to green
    subprocess.run(["nginx", "-s", "reload"])
```

### Strategy 3: Canary Deployment (Netflix / Google Use This)

```
Send 5% of traffic to new version. If no errors → increase to 100%.

  Load Balancer
        │
        ├── 95% → V1.0 (stable)
        │
        └──  5% → V2.0 (canary) ← Monitor for errors, latency

  If canary looks good:
    ├── 80% → V1.0
    └── 20% → V2.0

  Then:
    ├── 50% → V1.0
    └── 50% → V2.0

  Then:
    └── 100% → V2.0 ✅

  If canary shows errors:
    └── 100% → V1.0 (instant rollback)
```

```nginx
# Nginx canary config — split traffic by weight
upstream app_stable {
    server app-v1:8000;
}

upstream app_canary {
    server app-v2:8000;
}

split_clients "${remote_addr}" $upstream_variant {
    95%   app_stable;   # 95% to stable version
    *     app_canary;   # 5% to canary
}

server {
    location / {
        proxy_pass http://$upstream_variant;
    }
}
```

sections.title: 7. Performance Profiling
sections.body:
### Finding the Bottleneck Before Scaling

### Rule: Don't Scale What You Haven't Profiled

```
Common bottlenecks (in order of likelihood):
  1. N+1 Query Problem      ← 90% of perf issues
  2. Missing database index  ← Check EXPLAIN ANALYZE
  3. No caching             ← Add Redis
  4. Synchronous I/O        ← Use async
  5. Unoptimized serialization← Use orjson
  6. Actually need more servers ← LAST resort
```

### The N+1 Query Problem (Performance Killer #1)

```python
# ❌ N+1 PROBLEM — 101 queries for 100 orders!
@app.get("/orders")
async def list_orders(db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db)):
    orders = await db.execute(select(Order).limit(100))  # Query 1

    result = []
    for order in orders.scalars():
        # Each iteration = another query! (N queries)
        user = await db.execute(
            select(User).where(User.id == order.user_id)
        )
        result.append({
            "order": order,
            "user": user.scalar_one()
        })
    return result
    # Total: 1 + 100 = 101 queries! Takes 5-10 seconds 🐌

# ✅ FIXED — 1 query with JOIN
@app.get("/orders")
async def list_orders(db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db)):
    result = await db.execute(
        select(Order, User)
        .join(User, Order.user_id == User.id)
        .limit(100)
    )
    return [
        {"order": order, "user": user}
        for order, user in result.all()
    ]
    # Total: 1 query! Takes 10-50ms ⚡

# ✅ ALTERNATIVE — Eager loading with SQLAlchemy
from sqlalchemy.orm import selectinload

@app.get("/orders")
async def list_orders(db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db)):
    result = await db.execute(
        select(Order)
        .options(selectinload(Order.user))  # Load users in 1 extra query
        .limit(100)
    )
    return result.scalars().all()
    # Total: 2 queries (1 for orders, 1 for all users) ⚡
```

### FastAPI Request Profiling Middleware

```python
import time
import logging

logger = logging.getLogger("performance")

@app.middleware("http")
async def profile_requests(request: Request, call_next):
    """Log slow requests for investigation"""
    start = time.perf_counter()

    response = await call_next(request)

    duration_ms = (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000

    if duration_ms > 500:  # Log anything over 500ms
        logger.warning(
            f"SLOW REQUEST: {request.method} {request.url.path} "
            f"took {duration_ms:.0f}ms | "
            f"Status: {response.status_code}"
        )

    response.headers["X-Response-Time"] = f"{duration_ms:.0f}ms"
    return response
```

### SQL Query Logging (Find Slow Queries)

```python
import logging

# Enable SQLAlchemy query logging
logging.getLogger("sqlalchemy.engine").setLevel(logging.INFO)

# Or more precise — log only slow queries
from sqlalchemy import event

@event.listens_for(engine.sync_engine, "before_cursor_execute")
def before_execute(conn, cursor, statement, parameters, context, executemany):
    conn.info["query_start_time"] = time.time()

@event.listens_for(engine.sync_engine, "after_cursor_execute")
def after_execute(conn, cursor, statement, parameters, context, executemany):
    total = time.time() - conn.info["query_start_time"]
    if total > 0.1:  # Log queries taking > 100ms
        logger.warning(f"SLOW QUERY ({total*1000:.0f}ms): {statement[:200]}")
```

### Response Serialization (Hidden Performance Issue)

```python
# ❌ Default JSON serialization is SLOW for large responses
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse  # Uses standard json module

# ✅ Use orjson — 10x faster JSON serialization
# pip install orjson
from fastapi.responses import ORJSONResponse

app = FastAPI(default_response_class=ORJSONResponse)

# Benchmark:
# json.dumps(large_list):   ~50ms
# orjson.dumps(large_list): ~5ms  (10x faster!)
```

sections.title: 9. Graceful Degradation
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Check if feature is enabled
- Reject requests when system is overloaded
- Execute coroutine with timeout
- Feature flags — turn features on/off without deploying
- Percentage rollout (gradual release)
- Consistent — same user always gets same result
- Admin: Roll out to 10%
- If no issues → 50% → 100%

**Defines:** `FeatureFlags`, `get_feed()`, `get_product()`, `BackpressureMiddleware`, `with_timeout()`, `search()`

### When Things Go Wrong, Don't Crash — Degrade Gracefully

### Feature Flags (Deploy Without Risk)

```python
# Feature flags — turn features on/off without deploying

import redis.asyncio as redis

class FeatureFlags:
    def __init__(self, redis_client):
        self.redis = redis_client

    async def is_enabled(self, feature: str, user_id: str = None) -> bool:
        """Check if feature is enabled"""
        # Global toggle
        global_flag = await self.redis.get(f"feature:{feature}:enabled")
        if global_flag == "false":
            return False

        # Percentage rollout (gradual release)
        percentage = await self.redis.get(f"feature:{feature}:percentage")
        if percentage:
            # Consistent — same user always gets same result
            user_hash = hash(f"{feature}:{user_id}") % 100
            return user_hash < int(percentage)

        return global_flag == "true"

    async def enable(self, feature: str, percentage: int = 100):
        await self.redis.set(f"feature:{feature}:enabled", "true")
        await self.redis.set(f"feature:{feature}:percentage", str(percentage))

    async def disable(self, feature: str):
        await self.redis.set(f"feature:{feature}:enabled", "false")

flags = FeatureFlags(redis_client)

# Usage
@app.get("/feed")
async def get_feed(user: User = Depends(get_current_user)):
    if await flags.is_enabled("new_algorithm", user.id):
        return await get_feed_v2(user)  # New algorithm (testing on 10% of users)
    return await get_feed_v1(user)      # Stable algorithm

# Admin: Roll out to 10%
await flags.enable("new_algorithm", percentage=10)
# If no issues → 50% → 100%
# If problems → instant disable:
await flags.disable("new_algorithm")
```

### Fallback Responses (Never Show Errors to Users)

```python
@app.get("/products/{product_id}")
async def get_product(product_id: int):
    # Try primary source
    try:
        product = await db.get_product(product_id)
        await cache.set(f"product:{product_id}", product)
        return product
    except DatabaseException:
        pass

    # Fallback 1: Try cache
    try:
        cached = await cache.get(f"product:{product_id}")
        if cached:
            return {**cached, "_source": "cache", "_stale": True}
    except RedisException:
        pass

    # Fallback 2: Return minimal data
    return {
        "id": product_id,
        "status": "temporarily_unavailable",
        "message": "Product details being updated. Please refresh."
    }
```

### Backpressure (Don't Accept More Than You Can Handle)

```python
import asyncio
from fastapi import HTTPException

class BackpressureMiddleware:
    """Reject requests when system is overloaded"""

    def __init__(self, max_concurrent: int = 1000):
        self.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(max_concurrent)
        self.current_requests = 0

    async def __call__(self, request: Request, call_next):
        if self.semaphore.locked():
            # System at capacity — reject gracefully
            return JSONResponse(
                status_code=503,
                content={
                    "detail": "Server is busy. Please retry in a few seconds.",
                    "retry_after": 5
                },
                headers={"Retry-After": "5"}
            )

        async with self.semaphore:
            return await call_next(request)

# Usage
app.add_middleware(BackpressureMiddleware, max_concurrent=1000)
```

### Request Timeouts (Don't Let Slow Requests Pile Up)

```python
import asyncio

async def with_timeout(coro, timeout_seconds: float = 5.0):
    """Execute coroutine with timeout"""
    try:
        return await asyncio.wait_for(coro, timeout=timeout_seconds)
    except asyncio.TimeoutError:
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=504,
            detail=f"Request timed out after {timeout_seconds}s"
        )

@app.get("/search")
async def search(q: str):
    # If search takes > 5 seconds, return timeout instead of hanging
    results = await with_timeout(
        elasticsearch.search(q),
        timeout_seconds=5.0
    )
    return results
```

diagrams.title: Graceful degradation under load
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  load{"Load level"} -->|"normal"| full["Full experience"]
  load -->|"high"| d1["Turn off recommendations, serve cached feed"]
  load -->|"very high"| d2["Shed non-critical endpoints, queue writes"]
  load -->|"overload"| d3["Static fallback page, protect checkout and login only"]
  full --> m["Signals: p99 latency, error rate, queue depth"]
  m --> load
diagrams.explain: When demand exceeds capacity, a well-built system gets *worse*, not *down*. Features are ranked by importance; as latency and error rates climb, the least important are switched off (feature flags), caches serve slightly stale data, writes are queued and non-critical traffic is shed — so the core path (login, checkout, playback) keeps working.

sections.title: 10. CDN & Edge Computing
sections.body:
### Serve Static Content from the Nearest Location

```
Without CDN:
  User in Tokyo → Request → Server in US (200ms latency) → Response
  Each image, JS file, CSS = 200ms round trip!

With CDN:
  User in Tokyo → CDN Edge in Tokyo (5ms!) → Cached Response
  Only API calls go to US server

Speed improvement: 40-100x for static assets!
```

### CloudFront / CloudFlare Setup

```python
# FastAPI: Serve API only, static assets via CDN

# Don't serve static files from FastAPI in production!
# ❌ app.mount("/static", StaticFiles(directory="static"))

# ✅ Upload static files to S3/CDN, return CDN URLs
CDN_BASE = "https://cdn.yourapp.com"

@app.get("/products/{product_id}")
async def get_product(product_id: int):
    product = await db.get_product(product_id)
    return {
        **product,
        "image_url": f"{CDN_BASE}/products/{product.image_path}",
        "thumbnail_url": f"{CDN_BASE}/products/thumbs/{product.image_path}",
    }
```

### Cache Headers for CDN

```python
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse

@app.get("/products")
async def list_products():
    products = await get_products()

    response = JSONResponse(content=products)
    # Tell CDN to cache this for 5 minutes
    response.headers["Cache-Control"] = "public, max-age=300, s-maxage=300"
    # CDN will serve cached version to all users for 5 min
    return response

@app.get("/users/me")
async def get_profile():
    # Private data — NEVER cache in CDN
    response = JSONResponse(content=user_data)
    response.headers["Cache-Control"] = "private, no-cache, no-store"
    return response
```

sections.title: 11. Connection Management at Scale
sections.body:
### PgBouncer (PostgreSQL Connection Pooler)

```
Problem:
  10 app servers × 20 connections each = 200 DB connections
  PostgreSQL max_connections = 100 → CONNECTION REFUSED!

Solution: PgBouncer sits between app and PostgreSQL

  App Server 1 (20 conn) ─┐
  App Server 2 (20 conn) ─┤
  App Server 3 (20 conn) ─┼→ PgBouncer (manages 50 real connections) → PostgreSQL
  App Server 4 (20 conn) ─┤
  App Server 5 (20 conn) ─┘

  200 virtual connections → 50 real connections
  PgBouncer recycles connections between requests
```

```ini
# pgbouncer.ini
[databases]
mydb = host=postgres port=5432 dbname=mydb

[pgbouncer]
listen_port = 6432
listen_addr = 0.0.0.0
auth_type = md5
auth_file = /etc/pgbouncer/userlist.txt
pool_mode = transaction          # Release connection after each transaction
max_client_conn = 1000           # Accept up to 1000 app connections
default_pool_size = 50           # Only keep 50 real DB connections
min_pool_size = 10               # Always keep 10 ready
reserve_pool_size = 10           # Extra buffer for spikes
reserve_pool_timeout = 3         # Wait 3s before using reserve
```

### Graceful Shutdown (Don't Drop In-Flight Requests)

```python
import signal
import asyncio

class GracefulShutdown:
    """Handle shutdown without dropping requests"""

    def __init__(self):
        self.is_shutting_down = False
        self.active_requests = 0

    def start_shutdown(self):
        self.is_shutting_down = True

    async def wait_for_completion(self, timeout: int = 30):
        """Wait for active requests to finish"""
        for _ in range(timeout):
            if self.active_requests == 0:
                return
            await asyncio.sleep(1)
        print(f"Forcing shutdown with {self.active_requests} active requests")

shutdown = GracefulShutdown()

@app.middleware("http")
async def graceful_shutdown_middleware(request: Request, call_next):
    if shutdown.is_shutting_down:
        return JSONResponse(
            status_code=503,
            content={"detail": "Server is shutting down"},
            headers={"Retry-After": "5"}
        )

    shutdown.active_requests += 1
    try:
        return await call_next(request)
    finally:
        shutdown.active_requests -= 1

# Handle SIGTERM (sent by Docker/Kubernetes)
def handle_sigterm(signum, frame):
    shutdown.start_shutdown()
    asyncio.create_task(shutdown.wait_for_completion())

signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, handle_sigterm)
```

sections.title: 12. The Million-User Checklist
sections.body:
### Use this checklist when preparing for scale:

```
PERFORMANCE (Can it handle the load?)
  □ Load tested with Locust/k6 (2x expected peak)
  □ p95 response time < 500ms under load
  □ Error rate < 0.1% under load
  □ No N+1 queries (check SQLAlchemy logging)
  □ Database queries optimized (EXPLAIN ANALYZE)
  □ Using async/await for all I/O operations
  □ Using orjson for JSON serialization
  □ Connection pooling configured (min/max sizes)

SCALING (Can it grow?)
  □ Application is stateless (no in-memory state)
  □ Sessions stored in Redis (not memory/disk)
  □ Can run multiple instances behind load balancer
  □ Auto-scaling configured (CPU/memory triggers)
  □ Read replicas for read-heavy workloads
  □ CDN for static assets (images, JS, CSS)
  □ Redis caching for hot data (cache-aside pattern)

RELIABILITY (Does it stay up?)
  □ Health check endpoint (/health)
  □ Graceful shutdown (handle SIGTERM)
  □ Circuit breakers for external services
  □ Retry with exponential backoff
  □ Dead letter queue for failed jobs
  □ Rate limiting per user/IP/tier
  □ Backpressure (reject when overloaded)
  □ Request timeouts on all external calls

DEPLOYMENT (Can you deploy safely?)
  □ Zero-downtime deployment (rolling/blue-green)
  □ Feature flags for risky changes
  □ Rollback plan (< 5 min to rollback)
  □ Database migrations are backwards-compatible
  □ CI/CD pipeline with automated tests

OBSERVABILITY (Can you see problems?)
  □ Structured logging (JSON format)
  □ Request tracing (request ID in every log)
  □ Prometheus metrics exposed
  □ Grafana dashboards for key metrics
  □ Alerts for error rate, latency, CPU
  □ Distributed tracing (if microservices)
  □ Error tracking (Sentry)

SECURITY (Is it safe at scale?)
  □ Rate limiting prevents abuse
  □ Input validation on all endpoints
  □ SQL injection prevention (parameterized queries)
  □ CORS configured for your domain only
  □ HTTPS everywhere (SSL/TLS)
  □ Secrets in environment variables
  □ DDoS protection (CloudFlare/AWS Shield)
```

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.body:
```
1. PROFILE before you scale — find the real bottleneck first
2. LOAD TEST with Locust/k6 — prove it handles 2x expected peak
3. RATE LIMIT with token bucket — protect your system
4. AUTO-SCALE with Kubernetes — pay only for what you use
5. DEPLOY with zero downtime — blue-green or rolling updates
6. OBSERVE with Prometheus + Grafana — catch problems before users do
7. DEGRADE GRACEFULLY — feature flags, fallbacks, backpressure
8. CDN everything static — 100x faster for global users
9. PGBOUNCER for database connections — handle thousands of app connections
10. Start simple, scale what breaks — premature optimization is the root of evil
```
